talks.title: The past is prologue: Intel needs to evolve to survive
talks.teaser: Analysts investigate attack surfaces and defenses concerning The past is prologue: Intel needs to evolve to survive.
talks.summary:
Overview: Vizzy, founder of the Vertex Project and co-author of the original APT1 report, presents at HITCON on intelligence analysis evolution and why the discipline must adapt to survive.

Key Topics: The APT1 report's origins at Mandiant in 2013; Chinese espionage targeting aerospace, pharmaceutical, and technology sectors; existential threats from stolen R&D; and the future of cyber threat intelligence analysis.

Technical Details: Vizzy recounts identifying Unit 61398's multi-year campaign exfiltrating terabytes weekly from English-speaking businesses, from aerospace engine schematics to pharmaceutical research. The report established attribution methodology now standard in CTI.

Takeaways: CTI must evolve beyond indicator sharing to strategic analysis of adversary intent and impact. The APT1 model of public attribution changed the industry, but analysts must continue adapting methodologies.

talks.teaser: Engineers explore architecture and security mechanisms for ARTIPHISHELL Agents: LLM-Driven Bug Hunting & Patching in Open Source Software.
talks.summary:
DARPA AI Cyber Challenge

Will Gibbs and Lucas Dresl of the Shellphish multi-university team present their HITCON talk on LLM-driven autonomous bug hunting and patching for open source, built for DARPA's AI Cyber Challenge with roughly twenty-six contributors from ASU, UCSB, and Purdue.

Competition scope

AIC targets fully autonomous discovery and repair across hard codebases such as nginx, SQLite, Jenkins, and the Linux kernel. Semifinalists received two-million-dollar prizes; finals added larger awards. Motivations included prize money, giving back to open source, and learning bleeding-edge LLM security uses.

Pipeline overview

Their CRS narrows huge codebases using Semgrep and CodeQL queries, prioritizing delta-mode diffs where new changes introduce or expose bugs. Diffy generates targeted CodeQL queries around patches; Code Swipe heuristically weights candidate functions from diff proximity, static warnings, and reachability before LLMs analyze prioritized code for exploitable issues.

talks.title: Breaking Autonomy: Hacking Cloud-Native AI Agents
talks.teaser: Shows how prompt tricks, unvalidated tool inputs and poisoned memory let attackers hijack an AWS Bedrock agent and its sub-agents.
talks.summary:
This talk covers attacks on agents built with the AWS Bedrock agent framework, which links a language model to tools, knowledge bases and long-term memory. The speaker works through three goals against a single agent: extract its instructions and tool definitions, misuse those tools, and persist a working exploit in memory.

Direct requests for the system prompt were refused, but a reworded question about capabilities and rules exposed detailed tool descriptions. Once the agent was told to skip its input checks, a reversed vacation date range was accepted and raised one balance from 45 to 74 days, and a booking lookup tool was open to SQL injection that returned another user's reservation. For memory poisoning, a hidden instruction on a web page was saved to long-term memory during session summarization and later sent a user's booking details to an external server. The multi-agent section covered identifying supervisor or routing mode, listing sub-agents, and relaying payloads to them, including a ticket tool that issued a refund and free credit.

The closing advice is to read raw prompts and responses in traces, which show how the framework and model behave. Social engineering of the model can match prompt injection, and exact payload wording is unnecessary. Pre-processing, post-processing and the content filter are off by default over cost, latency and false positives, so production teams should enable them.

talks.title: Headphone Jacking: A Key to Your Phone
talks.teaser: Shows how exposed Bluetooth headphones can leak firmware and pairing keys, letting an attacker impersonate them to a phone.
talks.summary:
Dennis and Julian examine Bluetooth audio headphones and ask whether an ordinary pair can be turned into an attack device. Their starting point was a transmitter dongle whose USB HID protocol they captured in Wireshark and traced through its firmware to commands that write and read flash memory. The same protocol turned up over Bluetooth Classic RFCOM in the headphones' companion app, and over BLE GATT, and neither transport required pairing. Their tool dumped the full flash of the devices, including a connection table that held the names, addresses and link keys of paired phones.

With a phone's link key and the headphones' address, they showed they could impersonate the headphones to the phone using the hands-free profile. In a live demo they used a voice assistant to send a text message from the phone. They also described the scope of the problem: the chip family appears in a large number of flagship and budget products, with an estimate of around 100 possibly affected devices, while physical testing confirmed about 21.

The disclosure timeline followed. The chip vendor received a detailed report in March but did not reply for about a month, so the team contacted some device makers, and an SDK update arrived about a week after the vendor finally engaged. Partial details were presented at a conference in June, CVEs were published in August, and full technical details plus a check tool are planned for the end of the year. For users, the practical advice was to install headphone firmware updates, remove old pairings, or use wired headphones, because stored link keys stay usable even after a device is no longer in use.

talks.title: Resilience 2.0~ from firewalls to lifeboats
talks.teaser: Maps perimeter collapse, telecom attacks, and coordinated resilience practices for organizations facing Salt Typhoon-era threats.
talks.summary:
The presentation ties HITCON 2025’s perimeter-security theme to a return visit on cyber resilience, arguing that castle-style network boundaries have been inadequate for more than a decade as assets moved to cloud and SaaS, APIs multiplied, and edge appliances themselves became lucrative targets.

After aligning with the conference’s three resilience pillars—adapting to emerging threats, sustaining operations under attack, and recovering quickly—the speaker stresses that these functions must integrate across siloed governance, with communication security treated as essential. Case studies include a July 2025 Starlink outage affecting Ukrainian battlefield comms, the February 2022 Viasat/KA-SAT incident attributed to Russia via a VPN appliance misconfiguration that bricked tens of thousands of modems, Salt Typhoon’s alleged compromise of major U.S. carriers including lawful-intercept systems through critical Cisco flaws, and recent French telecom and Orange production impacts.

Compared with 2018, attack surface, IoT and ICS connectivity, AI-enabled deception, and LLM propaganda expand risk while monitoring visibility shrinks; weak MFA adoption—illustrated by Reddit’s SMS 2FA breach despite prior NIST warnings—remains a recurring gap. Q&A emphasizes vendor secure-by-design, rapid patching of security appliances, and faster uptake of government guidance across constituencies.

talks.title: Automating software security with LLMs
talks.teaser: Shows LLM agents finding, triaging and patching bugs in large open source projects, plus generating inputs that trigger them.
talks.summary:
The talk asks whether large language models can take over the work of finding, checking, patching and exploiting software bugs without a human in the loop. It starts with DARPA's 2016 Cyber Grand Challenge, where autonomous systems built on fuzzing and symbolic execution found and fixed bugs but offered little explanation of why their results could be trusted. It then moves to the later LLM-based challenge, which used full open source codebases instead of purpose-built targets.

The speaker explains the building blocks: a bare LLM, an agent made by looping tool calls, and a classifier that uses output probabilities to give graded confidence. The patching agent gets narrow code-reading tools built on static analysis, deterministic test runs after each change, and sub-agents for higher-level questions. For bug finding across millions of lines, single-shot prompts with very precise questions worked better than vague ones, and an iterative triage pipeline kept costs down by spending more only on reports that survived earlier stages. Proof-of-concept inputs were produced as Python input encoders, with separate agents handling harness choice, input structure and debugger feedback. In one FreeRDP case, the agent reached a zero-day signed integer overflow that fuzzing had never hit, in about 40 minutes and for roughly $4 of spend.

The closing advice is to do as much of the work yourself as you can, give agents only the tools a task needs, and run evaluations on your own use cases. The speaker argues that the main limit is the tooling built around current models rather than the models themselves.

talks.title: How (Not) to Metagame Pwn2own
talks.teaser: Walks through a Pwn2Own IoT campaign, covering target choice, draw-order payouts and a remote router kernel heap exploit.
talks.summary:
The speakers from Midnight Blue describe their experience in the IoT category of ZDI's Pwn2Own live zero-day competition in Ireland. They explain how the random draw order cuts payouts for later teams, and how bug collisions with other teams cut them further, which shapes how they choose targets. Their practical advice is to buy devices early, favour quantity over quality, and sign up for a target before an exploit is finished.

They then cover the targets that did not pay off. A Lua-based attempt on one device stalled after weeks of work, and a Synology format string bug was killed by a firmware update an hour before the signup deadline. On the successful side, they describe a Lexmark printer exploit built from a JPEG 2000 parser bug found by fuzzing, and an integer overflow in a custom JB2 parser found by code review. For a Synology B station, they describe an unsanitised metrics value that reached a root command through a Node.js server before authentication. For the QAP router, they show command injections and a remote kernel heap exploit in a deep packet inspection kernel module, with fuzzing done through a userland harness.

Their small office home office chain burned two router bugs to avoid collisions, but nine teams all chose the same router and the speakers placed fifth in the draw. Their closing takeaways are that draw order dominates payout, last-minute patches are part of the game, and burning bugs on fresh targets was not very effective.
